summary: This informational document explains Self-Delimiting Numeric Values, a field type that encodes arbitrarily large non-negative integers or bit strings compactly. The length is implied by the data, so protocols can grow without fixed field sizes. It was introduced in Delay-Tolerant Networking protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: An SDNV stores a non-negative integer in as many bytes as needed, with a bit in each byte showing whether more bytes follow. This lets a protocol encode small values compactly while allowing larger values when needed.

subtitle: A variable-length encoding for non-negative integers and bit strings.

tldr.problem: A fixed-width field can waste space when values are small or become too short as a protocol's values grow. Negotiating a wider field can also be costly in networks with long delays.
tldr.mechanism: A Self-Delimiting Numeric Value (SDNV) stores seven data bits per byte and uses the high bit to indicate whether another byte follows. The number of bytes grows with the encoded value.
tldr.outcome: The Informational RFC describes SDNV format, algorithms, limits, and trade-offs. A protocol using SDNVs must specify the maximum value size its implementations are expected to handle.

facts.label: Maximum size
facts.value: Must be specified by the protocol

today: RFC 6256 is an Informational IRTF document and the supplied metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: The Problem with Fixed-Width Fields
sections.content:
Protocol designers must choose how many bits to reserve for a value. A small field saves space but can later limit how a protocol is used; a larger fixed field can spend space even when the value is small. The RFC gives the TCP receive window and IPv4 address length as examples of fields whose sizes constrained later use.

SDNVs were introduced in Delay-Tolerant Networking protocols to avoid fixed field sizes and reduce unnecessary bytes. They can be useful where links have limited capacity and negotiation is undesirable, though the RFC does not recommend them for every field.
sections.plainLanguage: A fixed field size is a guess about how large a value will become. SDNVs let the field use more bytes only when the value needs them.

sections.title: How an SDNV Marks Its End
sections.content:
An SDNV represents a non-negative integer as a sequence of 7-bit groups. The high bit of each byte says whether it is the final byte: zero marks the end, while one means another byte follows. The low 7 bits carry the next part of the value.

For example, the value 1 uses one byte, 0x01. The value 128 uses two bytes, 0x81 0x00. During decoding, a reader collects each byte's low 7 bits and stops when it encounters a byte whose high bit is zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Each byte carries part of the number and a marker that says whether to keep reading. The reader stops at the first byte whose marker says it is last.

sections.title: Encoding, Decoding and Size Limits
sections.content:
To encode a value, the algorithm takes its low-order 7 bits, shifts the remaining value, and repeats while more bits remain. All bytes except the final one have the continuation bit set. Decoding shifts the accumulated value by 7 bits, adds the next byte's low-order bits, and continues until the final-byte marker appears.

The encoded length is not known until parsing is complete, so a decoder can run out of space or overflow if the value is too large. RFC 6256 says protocols must specify the largest SDNV size an implementation is expected to handle.
sections.plainLanguage: The encoder and decoder process the value in 7-bit pieces. A decoder needs a defined size limit so an unexpectedly large value cannot exceed its capacity.

sections.title: Trade-Offs and Safe Use
sections.content:
SDNVs use one overhead bit per byte, so the overhead is one eighth of the encoded bits. They may be inefficient for large values such as long cryptographic keys. The RFC notes that an SDNV can be useful as the length field in a type-length-value structure without directly encoding a large value.

Leading zero bits may be discarded during encoding and added during decoding. When encoding a bit field, a protocol must ensure both ends agree on the field width and meaning. Decoders should use bounds checks and handle values they cannot parse.
sections.plainLanguage: SDNVs save space for small values but add overhead for large ones. When they encode bit fields, sender and receiver need a shared understanding of the field's width.
